newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-Shorter work week mooted to give Bonn jobs for EMU.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Shorter work week mooted to give Bonn jobs for EMU.

text.p: Germany's largest union has proposed cutting the working week to create jobs amid warnings that economic developments crucial to Bonn's ability to qualify for Europe's monetary union are running behind forecast.

Economics Minister Guenter Rexrodt warned on Wednesday that although the German economy probably grew in the first quarter, there was no improvement on the labour market. He said growth must accelerate to meet Bonn's 1997 forecast of 2.5 percent.
Meanwhile new data from regional states showed that tax revenues so far this year have come in well below expectations.

The combination of slower than expected growth, a poor jobs market and lower than expected tax receipts could endanger Germany's bid to qualify for Europe's planned single currency by pushing its budget deficit above the target levels.

Doubts about Bonn's ability to keep its budget deficit from exceeding three percent, as required by the Maastricht treaty, has fuelled speculation that European economic and monetary union (EMU) would be delayed if Bonn failed to qualify.

With record unemployment currently ranked as Germany's top priority economic problem, a two-day jobs summit in Berlin ended with calls from union leaders for concrete action to create jobs by reducing working hours.

Klaus Zwickel, chairman of IG Metall, Germany's largest trade union, for the first time also made clear his union would be ready to accept a partial reduction in wages if employers agreed to the introduction of a 32-hour week.

Zwickel, who last year grabbed headlines by initiating a failed "Alliance for Jobs" pact with government and employers, said the first step to such a work reduction was the 35-hour week in the metal and engineering sectors it represents.

"A 35-hour week, together with a reduction in overtime and increased part-time work, must be introduced in all industry sectors," Zwickel told the 500-plus trade unionists, employers and politicians that attended the conference.
Engineering employers' group Gesamtmetall rejected the IG Metall proposal for a still shorter working week out of hand.
"Nowhere in the world is a cut in working time used as a means in the battle against unemployment," Gesamtmetall said.
"A general cut in working time has been consciously avoided in precisely those countries which have been more successful than Germany in maintaining and creating jobs," it added.
Independent analysts sided with the employers. "Zwickel's proposal is just a dead-end street," said Thomas Mayer, senior economist at Goldman Sachs in Frankfurt.

The sharp rise in German joblessness to over 4.5 million at the start of the year was the trigger for market worries that this would finally scupper Bonn's ambitions to keep its budget deficit below the three percent level.
Precise compliance with this goal is deemed essential in Germany, where the public is wary of exchanging the strong mark for the unknown quantity of a shared European currency.

Wolfgang Schaeuble, parliamentary head of the ruling Christian Democrats (CDU), stressed in an interview that Bonn, having insisted repeatedly that all would-be EMU members must hit this target on the nail, had to do so itself.

"We have all said since 1991 that the criteria must be strictly interpreted. A strict reading has been understood by most people as 3.0 percent," he told Stern magazine in an interview released ahead of publication on Thursday.
"Those who do not want to stand by that any more destroy the basis of confidence in the euro."
The comments by Schaueble, regarded as a likely successor to Chancellor Helmut Kohl, fuelled controversy within a coalition already straining to maintain a common line on EMU.
At the centre of several internal disputes stands Finance Minister Theo Waigel, whose stubborn line on the planned EMU worries politicians looking ahead to a series of elections next year.
In the coalition, the affable Bavarian is under pressure both to ease off and to tighten up on the Maastricht budget deficit target of three percent of gross domestic product.

The opposition Social Democrats (SPD), whose support will be needed to win parliamentary approval to join the single currency, are toying with the idea of running a Euro-sceptical campaign in the general election due in October 1998.
"We have to clear this up soon," said a strategist for Kohl's Christian Democratic Union (CDU).
But such worries may, in the end, prove to be of little concern to the powerful German Bundesbank, if the worst comes to the worst and Bonn misses the Maastricht deficit goal.

Analysts said that despite the rhetoric of some Bundesbank officials, the central bank council as a whole would not be worried if Germany narrowly missed meeting the goal in 1997, taking a longer-term view of the country's economic stability.

"The struggle over numerical targets is down to semantics," said Adolf Rosenstock, economist at the Industrial Bank of Japan. "From an economic standpoint the Bundesbank is not worried about Bonn's missing the target by a moderate amount."
